newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Environmental groups blast world trade body.
newsitem.headline: Environmental groups blast world trade body.

text.p: One of the world's leading environmental organisations accused governments on Sunday of opening the door to undermining major international agreements on protecting the earth in favour of trade.

The World Wildlife Fund for Nature (WWF) accused the 128-member World Trade Organisation (WTO), which opens its first ministerial meeting in Singapore on Monday, of "playing Russian roulette" with environmental agreements.
It said a WTO committee had recommended that members be allowed to take disputes on trade issues covered in international environmental agreements to the WTO panel.
"WTO members could resort to the WTO settlement mechanism to undermine obligations they have agreed to under environmental agreements," the WWF said in a statement.
"This is a realization of some of the worst fears of many environmental groups," it said.

"Instead of making trade and environment policies mutually supportive, the CTE is playing Russian roulette with them," it said, referring to the WTO's Committee on Trade and Environment (CTE), whose report it was criticising.

"They are expanding the WTO's legal jurisdiction by saying you can take two parties to environmental agreements to the WTO court which can judge between the two parties," WWF spokesman Charles Arden-Clarke told a news conference.
"They are putting the WTO in the hierarchy above multi-lateral environmental agreements," he said.
He said agreements at risk included the Montreal Protocol, which seeks to protect the ozone layer, and the Convention on the International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES).
The Friends of the Earth, another major environmental group, called on the WTO to close down the CTE and start afresh with much wider representation.
"The CTE is a waste of time and money and threatens to stand in the way of real environmental progress," it said.
"It's time to shut down the committee and move the debate to a new, open and independent forum, where ordinary citizens' voices can be hear," Friends of the Earth said in a statement.

Arden-Clarke said the WWF was not yet an advocate of closing the committee down but did agree it should be thrown open to non-governmental organisations (NGOs) deeply involved in environmental issues.
"This is big money, big politics. But they're still operating largely behind closed doors," he said.

"That means it's not only secret, but it's shutting itself off from important environmental issues on the ground. It has got to be more open and inclusive. It's got to include the NGOs on an equal footing."
At issue was sustainable development, including big industries like logging and fishing as well as protecting the environment from dirty industries, Arden-Clarke said.
He said the WTO committee was 80 strong, mostly trade officials, with fewer than 10 environmental experts.
Arden-Clarke gave no concrete examples of how environmental agreements could be undermined by the WTO committee's recommendation, but the WWF statement said the potential was undeniable.
"The CTE has set international trade law on a collision with international environmental law," it said.
"Such a dispute would seriously damage both legal regimes -- the environmental one in terms of effectiveness and the trade one in terms of public perception. Is the CTE serious?," it asked.
